extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical Euclidean geometry (learners, teachers, and practitioners studying circle theorems and constructions)
extracted.subtask_description: Selected propositions, definitions, and construction problems from Euclid's Elements (Books III–IV) concerning properties of circles, tangents, secants, intersecting chords, and constructions of inscribed/ circumscribed polygons and circles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Angle in a semicircle and in segments relative to right angle
rubrics_metrics.description: The angle in a semicircle is a right angle. The angle in a segment greater than a semicircle is less than a right angle. The angle in a segment less than a semicircle is greater than a right angle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: use diameter and centre to show that the angle subtended by the semicircle equals the sum of two base angles of an isosceles triangle and compare to an exterior angle; also use opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral equalling two right angles to deduce the comparisons. Corollary: if one angle of a triangle equals the other two, then it must be a right angle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tangent–chord theorem (angle between tangent and chord equals angle in alternate segment)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a straight line touches a circle at B, and from the point of contact a straight line BD is drawn cutting the circle, then the angle which BD makes with the tangent at B equals the angle in the opposite (alternate) segment of the circle (i.e., angle between tangent and chord equals angle in the alternate arc).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction in proof: through B draw BA perpendicular to the tangent EF to locate the centre on BA; use properties of semicircle to show related angles are right and then subtract the common angle to conclude DBF equals BAD (angle in alternate segment). The proof also uses that opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to two right angles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct segment on given line containing a given rectilineal angle (Prop. XXXIII)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a straight line AB and a rectilineal angle C, one can describe on AB a segment of a circle whose inscribed angle equals the given angle C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: if C is a right angle, bisect AB and draw semicircle. If not, construct at A an angle equal to C, draw a perpendicular at A, bisect AB, draw a perpendicular at the midpoint to AB and find its intersection G so that GA = GB; draw circle with centre G through A and B; the chord subtends the required angle because the constructed line through A is tangent and angle between tangent and chord equals the given angle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cut off a segment from a circle containing a given angle (Prop. XXXIV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a circle and a rectilineal angle D, one can cut off from the circle a segment that contains an angle equal to D.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: at a point B of the circumference draw a tangent EF, then on the tangent construct angle FBC equal to D; by the tangent–chord theorem the corresponding inscribed angle in the alternate segment (BAC) equals D, so the segment BAC is the required one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersecting chords theorem (product of segments equality) (Prop. XXXV)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two straight lines AC and BD within a circle cut one another at E, then the rectangle (product) of the segments AE·EC equals the rectangle (product) BE·ED.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof covers cases: when both lines pass through the centre (trivial equality), when one passes through the centre (use right triangles, squares and subtraction of common squares), and the general case (draw diameter through intersection and reduce to previous cases). The proof repeatedly uses properties of right triangles, equal segments from perpendicular bisectors, and adding/removing equal squares to compare rectangles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power-of-a-point for external point: tangent squared equals secant whole×external part (Prop. XXXVI)
rubrics_metrics.description: From a point D outside a circle, draw a secant DCA cutting the circle at A and C and a tangent DB touching the circle; then the rectangle AD·DC equals the square of the tangent DB (i.e., (whole secant)×(external part) = (tangent)^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof treats cases when the secant passes through the centre (use right triangles and equality of squares) and when it does not (drop perpendicular from centre to secant, use equalities of squares and add/remove equal squares), concluding that AD·DC = DB^2. Corollary: for two secants from same external point, the products of whole×external parts are equal because each equals the square of the tangent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Converse: equality of rectangle and square implies tangent (Prop. XXXVII)
rubrics_metrics.description: If from a point D outside a circle two straight lines are drawn, one cuts the circle and the other meets it, and the rectangle (whole×external part) of the cutting line equals the square of the meeting line, then the line which meets the circle is a tangent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof constructs the tangent DE from D and shows DE = DB (the given meeting line), and then by triangle congruence and right-angle reasoning concludes DB is perpendicular to radius when produced, hence DB touches the circle. Uses the uniqueness of tangents from an external point and that equality of squared lengths forces equality of lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of inscribed/ described figures and 'placed in' (Book IV definitions I–VII)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions: (I) rectilineal figure inscribed in another when all its angles lie on sides of the containing figure; (II) a figure described about another when its sides pass through the angular points of the inner figure; (III) rectilineal figure inscribed in a circle when all its angles are on the circumference; (IV) rectilineal figure described about a circle when each side touches the circumference; (V) circle inscribed in a rectilineal figure when its circumference touches each side; (VI) circle described about a rectilineal figure when its circumference passes through all angular points; (VII) a straight line is placed in a circle when its extremities lie on the circumference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are precise geometric definitions used to state and solve the subsequent construction problems. They govern language: 'inscribed', 'described about', and 'placed in' have exact meanings for constructions and proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place a straight line equal to a given line in a circle (Prop. I, Book IV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given circle ABC and straight line D not greater than the diameter, one can place in the circle a straight line equal to D.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: compare D with the circle's diameter BC; if equal place it; if BC greater, mark on BC a segment CE equal to D and with centre C draw circle through A so that CA = CE = D. Straightforward use of circle-centred construction to transfer length into circle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inscribe in a circle a triangle equiangular to a given triangle (Prop. II, Book IV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given circle ABC and triangle DEF, one can inscribe in ABC a triangle equiangular to DEF.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: draw a tangent at A, construct angles at A equal to the required angles (using tangent–chord theorem to relate), and select points on circumference so the subtended angles equal those of DEF, yielding triangle ABC equiangular to DEF.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe about a circle a triangle equiangular to a given triangle (Prop. III, Book IV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given circle ABC and triangle DEF, one can construct a triangle about the circle ABC that is equiangular to DEF (i.e., circumscribe a triangle around the circle with given angles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: find centre K, draw an arbitrary radius KB, construct angles at K equal to given triangle's external angles, then draw tangents at A,B,C accordingly to obtain triangle LMN equiangular to DEF. Uses properties of tangents and right angles at points of contact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inscribe a circle in a triangle (incenter construction) (Prop. IV, Book IV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given triangle ABC, construct a circle inscribed in ABC (the incircle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: bisect two angles by BD and CD meeting at D (incenter); from D drop perpendiculars to sides AB, BC, CA to locate points of tangency; these perpendiculars are equal so the circle centered at D with that radius touches all three sides. Proof uses angle bisector properties and right angles from centre to tangent points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe a circle about a triangle (circumcenter construction) (Prop. V, Book IV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given triangle ABC, construct the circumcircle that passes through A, B, C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: bisect AB and AC, draw perpendiculars to meet at F (circumcenter); FA = FB = FC hence circle with centre F passes through all vertices. Corollary: position of circumcenter relative to triangle indicates whether triangle is acute (center inside), right (center on hypotenuse), or obtuse (center outside).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inscribe a square in a circle (Prop. VI, Book IV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given circle ABCD, one can inscribe a square by drawing two diameters at right angles and connecting endpoints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: draw perpendicular diameters AC and BD; connect successive endpoints to form quadrilateral ABCD which is equilateral and rectangular hence a square. Proof uses equal radii and right angles subtended by semicircles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe a square about a circle (Prop. VII, Book IV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given circle ABCD, one can construct a square circumscribed about it (each side tangent to the circle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: draw perpendicular diameters, at each endpoint draw tangents (lines perpendicular to radius at contact), these tangents form a square. Proof shows corresponding sides are parallel and equal, and interior angles are right angles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inscribe a circle in a square (Prop. VIII, Book IV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given square ABCD, one can inscribe a circle that touches all four sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: bisect two adjacent sides and through these midpoint draw parallels to construct a smaller central square/parallelogram configuration whose centre is equidistant from sides; draw circle centered there with radius to midpoint to touch all sides. Uses right-angle tangency property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe a circle about a square (Prop. IX, Book IV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given square ABCD, one can draw a circumcircle passing through all four vertices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: join diagonals AC and BD meeting at E; EA = EB = EC = ED, so circle with centre E through any vertex passes through all four. Proof uses symmetry and equal triangles formed by diagonals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct an isosceles triangle with base angles double the vertex angle (Prop. X, Book IV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given segment AB, one can construct an isosceles triangle ABD such that each base angle is double the vertex angle at A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: pick point C on AB so rectangle AB·BC equals square of CA; describe circle and tangent constructions show BD touches a constructed circle, leading to isosceles ABD with desired angle relations. Proof uses the secant–tangent relation and equal-angle comparisons to deduce the doubling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inscribe an equilateral and equiangular pentagon in a circle (Prop. XI, Book IV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given circle ABCDE, one can inscribe a regular (equilateral and equiangular) pentagon in it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: construct an isosceles triangle with base angles double the apex angle (as in Prop. X), inscribe a triangle equiangular to it so that certain arcs are equal, bisect particular angles and join points to form pentagon ABCDE. Proof shows equal circumferences correspond to equal sides and equal angles, hence the figure is equilateral and equiangular.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe an equilateral and equiangular pentagon about a circle (start of Prop. XII, Book IV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given circle ABCDE, construct a regular pentagon circumscribed about the circle by drawing appropriate tangents so the sides are equal and angles equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposition begins by taking points with equal circumferences and drawing tangents GH, HK, KL, LM, MG at those points; the remainder of the construction and proof (not fully included in this chunk) follows by showing the tangents form an equal-sided, equal-angled pentagon about the circle. Uses prior propositions linking equal arcs to equal chords and tangent properties.
